features.normalized_proposition: febrile lower respiratory illness in infancy
diffuse and symmetric adventitious sounds rather than a focal area of altered air entry
Correct where the illness is not improving as expected, where severity raises the possibility of bacterial infection, or where a focal consolidation is demonstrated.
expiratory wheeze with increased work of breathing
a first episode of wheezing in an infant under twelve months
Correct in an older infant or child with frequent recurrences, atopy, or wheeze without a viral upper respiratory prodrome.
acute wheeze in an infant
symmetric air entry with no focal or unilateral findings
Correct where the onset is abrupt without a viral prodrome, or where findings are focal or asymmetric.
an oxygen saturation-based assessment of the same infant
a lower-risk infant who is feeding well and improving in work of breathing
Correct for a high-risk patient early in the course of the disease.
an investigation aimed at the same lower respiratory illness
a typical presentation with the diagnosis not in doubt
Correct where the diagnosis is unclear, improvement is not as expected, or severity raises the possibility of bacterial pneumonia.
a test ordered to characterise the same acute illness
a diagnosis already secure on clinical grounds
Correct where testing is required for infection control purposes, or in a high risk patient where the result will influence treatment.
a test ordered to decide whether more than supportive care is needed
a temperature that is not fever and an infant who is well perfused and feeding
Correct where clinical judgement raises a specific concern for serious bacterial infection.
delivery of supplemental oxygen through the nose
saturations that respond to a low flow rate
Correct in moderate to severe disease where non-invasive support is needed to avert continuous positive airway pressure or intubation.
a nebulized intervention aimed at the same respiratory distress
hypoxemia rather than airway narrowing as the problem to be corrected
Correct as a monitored single trial where a clinical response would justify continuing, chiefly in the emergency department.
a non-pharmacological supportive measure aimed at breathing
a saturation below the treatment threshold, which suction does not correct
Correct as an adjunct where nasal obstruction is limiting feeding or comfort, performed superficially and reasonably frequently.
a supportive intervention prescribed for the same admitted infant
an infant maintaining intake and hydration
Correct where the respiratory rate makes oral feeding unsafe or the infant is dehydrated.
a nebulized supportive measure in the same illness
hypoxemia as the problem, which airway hydration does not address
Not correct in a typical North American population, where it has no impact on length of stay.
a nebulized treatment for a wheezing infant
an explicit statement that the agent does not improve oxygen saturation
Not correct: bronchodilators do not improve oxygen saturation.
a tender indurated breast segment in a lactating patient
systemic signs such as fever, chills and tachycardia sustained beyond a day
Correct where there is focal induration with mild erythema and no systemic symptoms.
a painful swollen breast in the early postpartum period
unilateral segmental involvement rather than bilateral firmness
Correct with bilateral firmness and swelling around days three to five postpartum.
progressive induration and erythema of one breast segment
diffuse induration without a discrete fluctuant collection
Correct where a palpable fluid collection is present in a well-defined area of the breast.
a firm tender mass-like region of an inflamed lactating breast
an illness that has not yet been treated and worsened
Correct where a history of mastitis has worsened into a firm mass-like area without fluctuance.
a firm mass in a lactating breast
erythema and systemic symptoms, which a galactocele does not produce unless infected
Correct for a moderately firm mass without erythema or systemic symptoms, decreasing temporarily after a feed.
breast pain with induration in a lactating patient
systemic symptoms, which are uncommon in the subacute form
Correct with needle-like burning pain, nipple blebs and recurrent induration without systemic symptoms.
a red, swollen, firm breast
a first acute episode responding as an infection would
Correct with skin thickening, breast retraction and a peau d'orange appearance, or with recurrence in the same location.
a test ordered because the illness has not fully resolved on treatment
systemic symptoms that have improved on treatment
Correct where there is no symptomatic improvement after 48 hours of first-line therapy, or where a resistant organism is suspected.
cross-sectional imaging of a persistent breast mass
skin that shows no thickening, retraction or peau d'orange
Correct where the skin findings of inflammatory breast cancer are present, or where a mass persists after complete resolution of inflammation and needs malignancy work-up.
a test ordered to decide whether the process is still active
a structural question about a palpable mass
Not correct for this question: they are markers of inflammation and not specific for infection.
a procedure that would establish whether the mass is a fluid collection
a mass that has not yet been shown to be a fluid collection
Correct once a fluid collection is established, as the drainage step that achieves source control.
removal of milk from an inflamed breast
a feedback mechanism in which increased removal increases production
Not correct: overfeeding from the affected breast or pumping to empty perpetuates hyperlactation.
a manual technique applied to the inflamed segment
light sweeping of the skin rather than deep tissue pressure
Correct only as light sweeping that approximates manual lymphatic drainage.
an instruction about what the infant receives from the affected breast
an explicit statement that the milk is safe for the child
Not correct: bacterial mastitis is not a contraindication to breastfeeding.
a change to how the infant feeds from the affected breast
an instruction that does not address the underlying inflammation
Not correct: no evidence supports dangle feeding, and it is an unsafe infant position.
an instruction about how the infant latches to the affected breast
inadequate breast milk extraction, which worsens the underlying problem
Not correct: neither safety nor effectiveness has been demonstrated and shields result in inadequate milk extraction.
acute lower abdominal pain in a woman of reproductive age
maximal tenderness at McBurney's point rather than adnexal or cervical motion tenderness
Correct where the pelvic examination shows cervical motion tenderness or adnexal tenderness with lower abdominal tenderness.
acute unilateral lower abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting
a steadily progressive pain that migrated and then localised, rather than an intermittent one
Correct where there is an adnexal mass of five centimetres or more, or intermittent severe pain with a poorly localised or absent tenderness pattern.
fever with unilateral lower abdominal pain in a woman of reproductive age
an onset over hours that migrated, rather than the more gradual onset described for a tubo-ovarian abscess
Correct where the pain has been more gradual in onset with the pelvic findings of upper genital tract infection.
cross-sectional imaging of the right lower quadrant to settle an intermediate suspicion
a body mass index that is high rather than low
Correct in a low body mass index patient, and as the first modality in pregnancy.
cross-sectional imaging without ionising radiation
a non-pregnant patient, which is the stated indication for this modality
Correct in pregnancy when ultrasound is non-definitive.
a step that settles the diagnosis definitively
a score in the intermediate rather than the high band
Correct where clinical suspicion is high, particularly in a young male.
a strategy for resolving diagnostic uncertainty in the same patient
a patient who has not yet had the imaging the intermediate band calls for
Correct after non-diagnostic imaging, where clinical suspicion on reassessment is intermediate or low.
an initial imaging pathway for acute right-sided abdominal pain
a migratory pain with focal peritoneal signs rather than a colic pattern
Correct where a ureteral stone is the leading diagnosis.
a definitive management plan for acute appendicitis
perforation with generalised peritonitis rather than uncomplicated disease
Correct in selected adults with uncomplicated appendicitis who accept a cross-over and recurrence risk.
a strategy explicitly recommended for complicated appendicitis
free intraperitoneal fluid with generalised peritonitis rather than a walled-off collection
Correct where there is a phlegmon or a walled-off abscess at presentation.
a complete plan that ends in appendectomy
generalised peritonitis, which is not a disease that can be allowed to settle
Correct where operative management is contraindicated or the disease is walled off and settles on antibiotics.
a sustained depressive syndrome with functional impairment
a defined onset within the past year against a previously well baseline
Correct where two or more depressive symptoms have been present for more than two years.
recurrent depressive episodes with interepisode function
collateral history that records no distinct period of elevated mood or reduced need for sleep
Correct where a distinct and observable hypomanic period has occurred.
low mood with fatigue, weight change and psychomotor slowing
a normal thyroid stimulating hormone level
Correct where thyroid stimulating hormone is abnormal, or where somatic features point to an untreated endocrine cause.
fatigue and reduced activity in an adult
a normal complete blood count
Correct where the complete blood count is abnormal and the syndrome is explained by it.
an action taken to reduce imminent suicide risk
intent to act together with psychotic symptoms, the combination for which an inpatient setting is warranted
Correct alongside admission, and as a disposition in its own right for a patient who is not at high risk.
a step taken to settle the disposition of an at-risk patient
scales stated to have low sensitivity and predictive power for suicide behaviours
Correct only alongside clinician judgment, never as the determinant of disposition.
an action addressing the same depressive illness at the same visit
a delay of weeks to effect against a risk that is present tonight
Correct once safety is secured, as the treatment of the depressive episode.
a first-line acute treatment for the same moderate episode
a stated patient preference for medication
Correct where the patient prefers it and it is readily accessible, and preferred at mild severity.
an initial acute treatment plan containing an antidepressant
a moderate episode with low safety risk, for which the guideline frames the initial choice as between the two
Correct in severe episodes with high safety risk and without psychotic features, and where both modalities are available.
a first-line treatment named in the same guideline
a moderate rather than mild episode, at which this is adjunctive and second line
Correct as first-line monotherapy for mild depression, and as a second-line adjunct at moderate severity.
a first-line psychological treatment offered as the initial plan
a stated patient preference for medication rather than for a psychological treatment in any format
Correct where psychotherapy is the chosen modality and in-person delivery is not available.
longer measured survival in screen-detected cases without a treatment effect
an unchanged distribution of tumour grade or growth rate between the groups
Correct where the screened group contains a disproportionate share of slowly progressing variants of the disease.
an apparent survival benefit produced by the act of screening rather than by treatment
equal numbers of cases diagnosed in the two groups
Correct where more cases are diagnosed in the screened group than in the unscreened group.
a comparison that makes screening look better than it is
groups assembled by allocation rather than by choice, with comparable baseline health
Correct where the compared groups self-selected and differ in baseline health.
an edit to the same invitation letter
readers who perceive more authority than the recommendation carries may abdicate their right to informed consent
Correct where uptake, not autonomy, is the objective being optimised.
an edit to the same invitation letter
an edit that adds no information about benefit or harm
Correct where the aim is to improve uptake in a programme whose information content is already adequate.
an edit that adds numerical information to the letter
a count without a denominator, which does not give an individual reader a chance of benefit
Correct where the reader also has the denominator and the harms, so the figure can be interpreted.
an edit that adds performance information to the same letter
results that must be clearly interpretable to the person receiving them
Correct as programme documentation, where the audience can interpret the figures.
a decision about whether and how to start the programme
a confirmatory bottleneck that a smaller volume does not remove
Correct where the constraint is cost or logistics rather than an absolute shortfall in the confirmatory pathway.
a programme decision that changes how many people enter the confirmatory pathway
a threshold set too far toward the high-risk end will miss patients who could have benefitted
Correct where the current threshold sits too far toward the low-risk end and is generating avoidable low-yield referrals.
a complete programme decision about the launch
evaluation that measures harm after it has occurred rather than preventing it
Correct as a standing requirement of any programme that does launch.
a decision to hold the launch pending further work
a shortfall that is one of capacity rather than of cost-effectiveness
Correct where the open question is whether the programme represents value for money.
acute chest pain in an adult
the pain is exertional and pressure-like rather than pleuritic
Correct where pretest probability is raised by sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, hypoxemia or venous-thromboembolism risk factors, and the D-dimer or imaging pathway confirms it.
severe acute chest pain in an adult
the pain built up during exertion rather than being maximal at onset
Correct where the pain is abrupt and maximal at onset, or where a pulse deficit, an inter-arm blood pressure difference or malperfusion findings are present.
acute chest pain with an abnormal electrocardiogram
the pain is unchanged by posture and by deep inspiration
Correct where the pain is sharp, pleuritic and positional and the tracing shows widespread rather than territorial ST elevation or PR depression.
an immediate bedside action in an acute infarct
the blood pressure is already low
Correct for ischaemic pain in a patient whose physiology is not preload dependent and who is not hypotensive.
an action taken in response to the elevated jugular venous pressure
the lung fields are clear with no crackles and no oxygen requirement
Correct where the raised filling pressure is accompanied by pulmonary congestion in a patient who is not preload dependent.
an early pharmacological step in the management of an acute infarct
the patient is in a low-output state with a blood pressure of 84/56 mmHg
Correct after stabilization, once the patient is out of a low-output state and is not at risk of cardiogenic shock.
an intervention that raises the blood pressure in an acute infarct
the peripheries are warm, the patient is alert and urine output is maintained, so there is no end-organ hypoperfusion

Correct where acute-myocardial-infarction cardiogenic shock is present, that is persistent hypotension or a vasopressor requirement with end-organ hypoperfusion, alongside emergency revascularization.
a reperfusion strategy that ends in angiography
the estimated first-medical-contact-to-device time is about four hours
Correct where device therapy is reachable inside the accepted interval, or where an absolute contraindication prohibits fibrinolysis.
fibrinolysis given now at the referring centre
routine rapid transfer follows lysis rather than waiting on failure
Correct as a description of rescue intervention, which is what happens when reperfusion fails; it is not the whole strategy when reperfusion succeeds.
fibrinolysis given now
angiography follows successful fibrinolysis within twenty-four hours rather than several days later
Correct for an elective investigation of stable coronary disease, not for the angiography that follows successful fibrinolysis in an acute infarct.
a plan for further cardiac assessment
a rise and fall in troponin with dynamic ST- or T-wave change is a high-risk criterion even when symptoms resolve
Correct for a lower-risk or diagnostically uncertain presentation without a troponin rise and fall or dynamic tracing change.
keeping the patient in hospital rather than sending her home
the syndrome is already confirmed and high risk, so observation without an invasive plan is not the reserved option
Correct where the presentation is diagnostically uncertain rather than a confirmed high-risk syndrome.
arranging specialist cardiac assessment
confirmed high-risk non-ST-elevation syndrome requires admission rather than outpatient follow-up
Correct for a lower-risk presentation being worked up as an outpatient.
admission to hospital
the required inpatient strategy is an early invasive one, not non-invasive testing, once high-risk criteria are met
Correct where the presentation is diagnostically uncertain and non-invasive testing would settle it.
